## Proof

We claim that \(f(z)=\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{e^{tz}}{1+t^{2}}\,dt\) is defined and holomorphic on the **entire complex plane** \(\mathbb{C}\).

### Step 1. The integral is defined for every \(z\in\mathbb{C}\).

For \(t\in[-1,1]\) we have \(1+t^{2}\ge 1>0\), so the denominator never vanishes and the integrand \(g(t,z)=\frac{e^{tz}}{1+t^{2}}\) is continuous on \([-1,1]\times\mathbb{C}\). Fix \(z\in\mathbb{C}\). On the compact interval \([-1,1]\),

\[
|e^{tz}|=e^{t\,\mathrm{Re}(z)}\le e^{|z|},
\]

so

\[
\left|\frac{e^{tz}}{1+t^{2}}\right|\le \frac{e^{|z|}}{1+t^{2}}\le e^{|z|}.
\]

Thus the integrand is bounded by the constant \(e^{|z|}\) on \([-1,1]\), and the integral converges (absolutely) for every \(z\in\mathbb{C}\). Hence \(f\) is defined on all of \(\mathbb{C}\).

### Step 2. \(f\) is holomorphic on \(\mathbb{C}\) (i.e., \(f\) is entire).

We verify the hypotheses of the standard theorem on holomorphicity of parameter-dependent integrals (equivalently, we justify differentiation under the integral sign via locally uniform domination).

- For each fixed \(t\in[-1,1]\), the map \(z\mapsto e^{tz}\) is entire, hence \(g(t,\cdot)\) is holomorphic on \(\mathbb{C}\).
- The partial derivative with respect to \(z\) is
  \[
  \frac{\partial g}{\partial z}(t,z)=\frac{t\,e^{tz}}{1+t^{2}},
  \]
  which is continuous on \([-1,1]\times\mathbb{C}\).
- **Local uniform domination.** Let \(K=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|\le R\}\) be an arbitrary compact disk. For \((t,z)\in[-1,1]\times K\),
  \[
  \left|\frac{\partial g}{\partial z}(t,z)\right|=\frac{|t|\,|e^{tz}|}{1+t^{2}}\le \frac{|t|\,e^{|t||z|}}{1+t^{2}}\le \frac{1\cdot e^{R}}{1}=e^{R},
  \]
  where we used \(|t|\le 1\) and \(|t|/(1+t^{2})\le 1/2\le 1\) on \([-1,1]\). The constant \(e^{R}\) is integrable over \([-1,1]\) and independent of \(z\in K\).

By the dominated-convergence argument applied to the difference quotients (or equivalently by the holomorphic-parameter-integral theorem), differentiation under the integral sign is justified on every compact disk \(K\), and

\[
f'(z)=\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{t\,e^{tz}}{1+t^{2}}\,dt
\]

exists for every \(z\in\mathbb{C}\). Since \(R\) was arbitrary, \(f'\) exists on all of \(\mathbb{C}\), so \(f\) is holomorphic on \(\mathbb{C}\).

### Conclusion

The function \(f\) is defined and holomorphic on the **entire complex plane**:

\[
\boxed{\,\mathrm{Dom}(f)=\mathbb{C}\,}.
\]

### PROOF COMPLETE
